one_liner: Small scalar multiply-rotate hash with 64/128/256-bit output; beats HighwayHash-128/256 and FarmHash-128 only on short-key latency.
what_it_does: Rainbow is a non-cryptographic hash that returns a 64-, 128- or 256-bit digest from one function, rainbow::rainbow<hashsize, bswap>(data, len, seed, out), with a 64-bit seed. The repo also ships an incremental HashState (initialize with the total length, update, finalize), the rainsum CLI (sha256sum-like, Rainbow-256 by default in the code), a WASM/npm build (@dosyago/rainsum) with identical digests, and Rainstorm, a separate, slower, unvetted crypto-style hash. It is a new digest, not an API or output match for HighwayHash or FarmHash.
how_it_is_fast: State is four 64-bit lanes seeded with seed+length. Each 16-byte block is added to and subtracted from the lanes, then the code alternates mixA (two independent chains of multiply by an odd 64-bit prime, rotate, multiply, with xor coupling; eight multiplies) and mixB (four multiplies, seed injection, lane rotation, added in v3.7.1 after issue #79 showed no downward data flow). Keys under 16 bytes skip the loop and take only four mix calls plus the tail for a 64-bit digest (one or five more for 128 or 256 bits), which is why short-key latency is competitive; there is no SIMD, AES or 128-bit multiply, so bulk speed stays at about 1.28 bytes/cycle (12 dependent-chain multiplies per 32 bytes).
when_to_use: You need a 128- or 256-bit non-crypto digest of short keys (1-31 bytes) in portable scalar C++ and currently use HighwayHash-128/256 or FarmHash-128.CM: SMHasher3 shows 62.06 vs 99.09 and 69.61 cycles (128-bit) and 103.65 vs 154.48 cycles (256-bit).
You want one roughly 140-line Apache-2.0 function whose 64-, 128- and 256-bit variants each pass all 250 SMHasher3 tests.
Native C++ and browser/Node code must produce the same digests (the npm WASM build is checked against the same test vectors).
Big-endian targets that must match little-endian digests (the bswap template parameter normalizes loads and stores).
when_not_to_use: Bulk hashing of large buffers: 1.27-1.28 bytes/cycle against HighwayHash 2.87, FarmHash-128.CM 2.61, a5hash-128 6.92, MuseAir-128 7.15, MeowHash 12.43 and XXH3-128 12.72 on the same SMHasher3 page.
64-bit hash-table keys: rainbow-64 takes 61.63 cycles on short keys and 1.28 bytes/cycle, against rapidhash 30.41/8.82, wyhash 29.31/6.98 and XXH-64 52.60/3.99.

Picking the fastest passing 128- or 256-bit hash: a5hash-128 and MuseAir-128 beat rainbow-128 on both short keys and bulk, and RH512 (256-bit, 250/250 passing) beats rainbow-256 on both (79.73 cycles and 2.50 bytes/cycle vs 103.65 and 1.28).

Anything adversarial (MACs, integrity against attackers, HashDoS resistance): Rainbow is explicitly non-cryptographic, no keyed-hash claim is documented, and the sibling Rainstorm is unvetted with a published reduced-round collision.
Long-term stored digests: the README says hash definitions may evolve, and v3.7.1 already changed Rainbow's mixing after issue #79.

integration.dependencies: none for the hash (src/rainbow.cpp + src/common.h); the rainsum CLI also needs cxxopts, zlib and OpenMP
integration.min_toolchain: C++17 per the README; the Makefile builds with -std=c++20 -O3 -march=native using Homebrew LLVM clang++ on macOS
integration.platforms: any 64-bit-multiply target, little- or big-endian (endianness from GCC/Clang __BYTE_ORDER__); WASM via Emscripten
integration.thread_safety: single-call rainbow() is a pure function with no global state (reentrant); a HashState instance must not be shared between threads

gotchas: Harness flaw in the README's C++ vs WASM table (4x-23x): scripts/bench.mjs times whole child processes (./rainsum FILE vs node ./js/rainsum.mjs FILE) once per row, and the C++ side reads the file through std::istreambuf_iterator into a vector before hashing. The 10 B to 1 MB rows are all about 5-7 ms vs 127 ms, which is Node and process start-up; subtracting the 10-byte row, the 100 MB row implies about 2.3 GB/s native vs 1.3 GB/s WASM, roughly a 1.8x gap (derived from page data). The record's '4x to 23x slower' tradeoff should not be read as hash speed.

The README headline 'fastest 128-bit hash, and the fastest 256-bit hash' is false on the SMHasher3 page it links: rainbow-128 is dominated by a5hash-128 and MuseAir-128, and rainbow-256 by RH512, on both short-key cycles and bulk bytes/cycle.

The README says to link rainbow.o, but rainbow::rainbow is a file-static template, so the object exports nothing callable; the repo's own CLI #includes rainbow.cpp. The Makefile hard-codes /opt/homebrew/opt/llvm clang++, xcrun -isysroot, -fopenmp and -march=native, so Linux builds need edits.

The streaming HashState was dead code that ignored every update after the first until 2026-07-27; it now matches the single-call hash but must be initialized with the total length, so it cannot hash a stream of unknown length. The README option list says the CLI defaults to Rainstorm while the code defaults to Rainbow, and open issue #170 reports that stream mode appends a text label to binary output.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick Rainbow over a5hash or MuseAir only when you specifically need a 256-bit non-crypto digest from scalar code with matching native and WASM builds; for 64-bit keys rapidhash, wyhash or a5hash are about 2x faster on short keys, and for bulk data MeowHash (12.43 bytes/cycle), XXH3 (12.72) and AquaHash (15.84) are about 10-12x faster on the same SMHasher3 page.
verified_claims_summary: SMHasher3's maintainer-run results table (Rainbow v3.7.1, CPU, compiler and flags unstated, cycles converted at a nominal 3.5 GHz) lists rainbow-128 at 62.06 cycles/hash on 1-31-byte keys vs HighwayHash-128 99.09 and FarmHash-128.CM.seed1 69.61, and rainbow-256 at 103.65 vs HighwayHash-256 154.48; in bulk (262144-byte keys) Rainbow is 1.27-1.28 bytes/cycle, about half of HighwayHash and FarmHash-128.CM. The repo has no benchmark against any other hash; its own table only compares its C++ CLI with its WASM CLI.
status_note: Actively developed (last commit 2026-09-15, recent work is Rainstorm cryptanalysis), Apache-2.0 and small enough to vendor as two files, but the speed headline overstates the SMHasher3 data and Rainbow digests have changed between versions.
